```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "The deciding factor is the 90-day paying-customer constraint. Idea B handles PHI, so it must act as a HIPAA Business Associate from day one. That means signed BAAs, a documented risk assessment, and audited infrastructure, with a sourced year-one cost estimate of $8,000-$25,000. Brief B itself calls this 'difficult to reconcile' with a one-person, short-timeline build. Idea A's regulatory overhead is a 1-2 hour legal consult for a privacy policy and ToS, plus export/delete mechanisms.",
    "Idea B's demand evidence argues against B's own product. Brief B concedes that 'none of the sourced complaints are about a missing notes+reminders product.' The pain is about price and group-practice scaling (supervision sign-off, intern billing, couples records), and a minimal notes+reminders app does not address the scaling issues. The brief also notes that switching interest is flowing 'toward other full EHRs, not toward stripped-down tools.'",
    "Idea B's cheapest acquisition path is weak. Paid directory placement has a sourced $500/mo minimum. The free channel, r/therapists, is described as constrained by self-promotion norms and unproven for conversion. Idea A has sourced, flexible channels: a Product Hunt launch at $200-$2,000 and YouTube sponsorships at $20-$40 CPM. Brief A also cites organic community growth as the proven path for Obsidian.",
    "Idea A can be built by one person with AI agents. Brief A notes that its technical core (search, embeddings, linking, summarization) is now commodity via foundation-model APIs. Idea B can plausibly be built too, but its compliance requirements cannot be handed off to agents in the same way.",
    "Idea B's real advantages do not outweigh this. It has a higher price point ($29-$69/mo vs. $10-15/mo), a business-expense buyer, and a documented segment unhappy with incumbent pricing. But these help only after clearing a compliance gate that likely falls outside a 90-day solo window."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea B's demand evidence is its weakest point. The Reddit and competitor-blog quotes ('overkill', 'criminal' pricing, 'really expensive for what it offers') show dissatisfaction with SimplePractice's price. They do not show that anyone wants a stripped-down notes+reminders app, and Brief B itself says switching is going toward other full EHRs. Two competitor price points (TheraSoft $69/mo, TheraFocus $199/mo) also have no source URL, so they count as missing, which weakens the pricing landscape used to justify the $29-$69 range.",
  "confidence_note": "Low-to-moderate confidence. Neither brief separates cleanly, and A wins mainly because B has a hard blocker (HIPAA cost and obligations), not because A has strong positive evidence. A's own demand evidence is thin: one 2020 HN comment and one blog post, neither showing willingness to pay. A's competitive position is poor, with a free incumbent (Obsidian), a funded prior attempt at the same pitch (WorldBrain Memex), and Tana's pivot, which suggests weak monetization of pure PKM. A also concedes that its core feature (connecting more sources) may not address the actual churn driver (retrieval and habit). A at $10-15/mo can more plausibly land a first paying customer within 90 days, but it may never become a durable business. If B's HIPAA burden could be legitimately reduced (for example, a reminders-only tool storing no PHI), the judgment could flip."
}
```
